item.title: "Fascinating": Gillespie reacts to Khawaja's bombshell on Australia's 2018 sandpaper scandal
item.description: Australian legend Jason Gillespie has described Usman Khawaja's revelation about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal as "fascinating", particularly his claim that he had urged the entire Australian team ...
item.content:encoded:
"Fascinating": Gillespie reacts to Khawaja's bombshell on Australia's 2018 sandpaper scandal Australian legend Jason Gillespie has described Usman Khawaja's revelation about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal as "fascinating", particularly his claim that he had urged the entire Australian team to take collective responsibility for the incident in a dressing-room meeting. ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 10:19 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 10:19 IST

Jason Gillespie (Photo: Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Australian legend Jason Gillespie has described Usman Khawaja's revelation about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal as "fascinating", particularly his claim that he had urged the entire Australian team to take collective responsibility for the incident in a dressing-room meeting. Eight years after the infamous Sandpapergate scandal, Usman Khawaja dropped a bombshell on Saturday, claiming that the entire Australian team, including players and support staff, was involved in the 2018 ball-tampering incident during the South Africa tour. "Usman claims that he went and addressed the whole team and said, 'We need to take collective responsibility for this.' He said everyone was in that room. So, I found that really fascinating," Gillespie said in a video posted by ABC Sports on X. Until now, the widely accepted account of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, maintained by Cricket Australia (CA) and those involved, was that Steven Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were the only players responsible. Smith and Warner received 12-month bans from international and domestic cricket, while Bancroft was handed a nine-month suspension. "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us. In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now," Khawaja told Nine as per Cricinfo. Khawaja said he had urged the Australian team to take collective responsibility for the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, insisting that everyone knew what was happening. He expressed disappointment that Smith, Warner and Bancroft were left to shoulder the blame, adding that Warner had faced repeated criticism over the past eight years while remaining silent. "Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we had to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance. Obviously, it didn't work that way, and those three guys got crucified. I've seen Davey over the last eight years just get nailed bad over and over again, and it's taken a big man not to say anything and just to stay quiet," Khawaja added. (ANI)

item.description: President Trump stated that the US is talking to Iran while imposing sanctions on eight Canadian businesses accused of moving money for Tehran through crypto networks. Trump claimed military success ...
item.content:encoded:
Trump says US talking to Iran amid sanctions push President Trump stated that the US is talking to Iran while imposing sanctions on eight Canadian businesses accused of moving money for Tehran through crypto networks. Trump claimed military success and open shipping lanes, while the Treasury targeted financial channels linked to Iran and drug proceeds. ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 10:05 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 10:05 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

United States President Donald Trump saidthat Washington was talking to Iran, while his administration rolled out fresh sanctions targeting eight Canada-based money services businesses accused of assisting Tehran in routing funds through cryptocurrency networks. "We're talking to Iran. We have been," Trump told reporters before departing the White House. The American leader depicted the prevailing military situation as advantageous for Washington, adding that the strategic Strait of Hormuz was now opening. "We've beaten Iran. We are doing very well with Iran," he said. When questioned about his message to Iran, Trump interwove his assertion of military success with signals that diplomatic contacts remained active. These remarks coincided with the US Treasury Department's announcement of sanctions against eight Canada-based money services businesses under Operation Economic Outcast. The Treasury accused these commercial entities of swapping Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets to channel cross-border transfers involving Tehran. Officials asserted that numerous firms interacted with blacklisted Iranian crypto platforms or digital wallets tied to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The punitive steps were executed in tandem with Canada's financial intelligence unit, FINTRAC, alongside the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and the Drug Enforcement Administration, according to Treasury disclosures. The formal sanctions announcement omitted any characterisation of the measures as components of a negotiated arrangement and did not link the official designations to the contacts referenced by Trump. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott stated that Washington intended to persist in targeting revenue which it alleged provided backing for weapons programmes and regional proxies. He underscored that the initiative demonstrated collaborative efforts alongside Ottawa aimed at safeguarding North American financial infrastructure. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent emphasised that his department would track down Iran's financial channels across any global jurisdiction where they operated. Furthermore, the Treasury alleged that several designated outfits processed narcotics proceeds connected to former Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding. These claims appeared within the official designation documents; the review materials available did not contain statements from the accused enterprises. The imposed measures freeze targeted assets under American jurisdiction and bar US citizens from conducting commercial interactions with them, barring official waivers. These administrative actions do not amount to a criminal conviction. (ANI)

item.title: Usman Khawaja drops bombshell on 2018 sandpaper scandal, says "all of us" knew about ball-tampering
item.description: Former Australian batter Usman Khawaja has claimed that the entire Australian team, including players and support staff, was involved of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal during the South Africa tour.
item.content:encoded:
Usman Khawaja drops bombshell on 2018 sandpaper scandal, says "all of us" knew about ball-tampering Former Australian batter Usman Khawaja has claimed that the entire Australian team, including players and support staff, was involved of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal during the South Africa tour. ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 10:02 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 10:02 IST

Usman Khawaja. (Photo: Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Former Australian batter Usman Khawaja has claimed that the entire Australian team, including players and support staff, was involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal during the South Africa tour. He said the responsibility was collective, contrary to Cricket Australia's findings that implicated only Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft. Khawaja stressed that he had expected the truth to emerge over the past eight years and spoke out to ensure the three players were not left carrying the blame alone. Until now, the widely accepted account of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, maintained by Cricket Australia (CA) and those involved, was that Steven Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were the only players responsible. Smith and Warner received 12-month bans from international and domestic cricket, while Bancroft was handed a nine-month suspension. "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us. In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now," Khawaja told Nine as per Cricinfo. "Maybe I thought Davey would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn't think it was going to come down to this. But the longer it's gone on for, and right from the very start, I've been on the train of collectively taking it," he added. Khawaja said he had urged the Australian team to take collective responsibility for the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, insisting that everyone knew what was happening. He expressed disappointment that Smith, Warner and Bancroft were left to shoulder the blame, adding that Warner had faced repeated criticism over the past eight years while remaining silent. "Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we had to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance. Obviously, it didn't work that way, and those three guys got crucified. I've seen Davey over the last eight years just get nailed bad over and over again, and it's taken a big man not to say anything and just to stay quiet," Khawaja added. Khawaja highlighted the lasting impact of the 2018 scandal on Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith. He noted that Bancroft has struggled to regain his place in the Test side despite consistently scoring runs, while Smith successfully rebuilt his career but has never forgotten the events of that year. "And then 'Bangers' [Bancroft], in the same note, particularly, he played a little bit of Test cricket after that, but then never came back in, even though he's been scoring a lot of runs. He's been a terrific cricketer for a long time, but I know it's something that hangs over his head," Khawaja said. "Even Steve Smith. Steve's lucky, the greatest batsman of my generation. He came back from that, and he's come back as good as he ever was in that first Ashes series, and it's kind of been forgotten for him in some respects. But I know he has never forgotten that year and how it all panned out," he added. Khawaja said he spoke out because he believed Smith, Warner and Bancroft deserved justice and should not continue bearing the blame alone. He added that none of the three wanted to break their silence, fearing their accounts would be dismissed as hearsay, which prompted him to speak on their behalf. "But I'm not doing this for any other reason than I think it's the right thing to do. I've always felt like there's more to life than just cricket, and these guys, in some respect, deserve that justice. And it just doesn't feel like anyone's going to give it to them. None of those three wants to be the first to say anything. And rightly so, it will just be hearsay and 'their word' if they do. They needed someone else to say something," he said. Khawaja also revealed that Cricket Australia never interviewed him during its investigation into the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. The probe, led by then head of integrity Iain Roy and team performance manager Pat Howard, followed the Cape Town Test and resulted in sanctions against Smith, Warner and Bancroft. "I was sitting next to Cam Bancroft that whole Test match, and I didn't get interviewed. I thoroughly feel that I didn't get interviewed because of that, because they knew that I wanted to take it as a team, because they knew I was ready to tell the truth if I was interviewed," he concluded. (ANI)

item.title: JD Vance spearheads quiet diplomatic push for new Iran deal: Report
item.description: US Vice President JD Vance has been leading indirect negotiations with Iran to broker a ceasefire and revive nuclear talks. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump remains open to diplomacy, though military ...
item.content:encoded:
JD Vance spearheads quiet diplomatic push for new Iran deal: Report US Vice President JD Vance has been leading indirect negotiations with Iran to broker a ceasefire and revive nuclear talks. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump remains open to diplomacy, though military options remain ready if needed. ANI | Updated: 07-11-2026 10:01 IST | Created: 07-11-2026 10:01 IST

US Vice President JD Vance (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

United States Vice President JD Vance has spent the past fortnight directly engaged in indirect negotiations with Iran aimed at brokering a new ceasefire and resuming stalled nuclear discussions, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter. The US vice president's direct involvement elevates the indirect track to the administration's highest echelons, underscoring an initiative by Vance to extricate Washington from a conflict he explicitly blamed for the Republican Party's crushing electoral defeats this week. According to US officials and regional sources cited by Axios, US President Donald Trump currently remains amenable to letting diplomatic efforts proceed to test whether an agreement can be forged. "We're talking to them," Trump told reporters on Friday when asked about his message to Iran. Nonetheless, insiders cautioned that should Trump alter course and mandate renewed military action, US forces stand fully prepared to launch strikes on an expedited schedule. Behind closed doors, Vance has maintained daily discussions with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Pakistan's Army Chief Asim Munir and other mediators, Axios reported. White House special envoy Steve Witkoff and presidential adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner are likewise engaged in the diplomatic track. Well-informed sources revealed that Vance, alongside Qatari and Pakistani interlocutors, has evaluated setting up a working-level technical meeting involving American and Iranian delegates soon, though such a meeting has not yet materialised. The office of the US vice president chose not to issue any statements concerning the ongoing talks. Vance emerged as the most doubtful voice among Trump's inner circle before the war's outbreak in late February, persistently pushing for a diplomatic resolution. He previously headed the US negotiating team during an April summit focused on Iran held in Islamabad and played a central role in securing the bilateral memorandum of understanding last June. Vance later led the American delegation for direct talks hosted in Switzerland, which led Tehran to pledge that UN inspectors would be welcomed back to nuclear facilities. However, the resulting agreement collapsed shortly afterwards when units of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps resumed attacks on commercial shipping. The current diplomatic momentum began gathering pace a fortnight ago when Vance dispatched a formal letter addressed to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a close confidant of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, proposing the resumption of direct talks. Iranian representatives signalled that Vance's communication generated favourable momentum towards reviving negotiations. On Wednesday, Vance reasserted that the conflict constituted the primary driver behind voters' rejection of the GOP. While participants involved in the ongoing mediation characterised headway as being made, they depicted the overall pace as extremely sluggish. Diplomatic engagement persisted on Friday morning as Trump conferred with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani concerning Doha's efforts to bridge gaps dividing Washington and Tehran. Via an official release from his secretariat, Sheikh Tamim underscored the imperative to "continue dialogue and pursue diplomatic means to resolve differences, spare the region further escalation, and ensure freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies." (ANI)
